subject: forestSpirit
pitch: A small forest spirit, part deer and part mossy stone. A body of grey river stone covered in soft green moss, slender wooden legs ending in little hooves, branching antlers sprouting tiny white flowers and leaves, a pale wooden mask-like face with two glowing green eyes, and a few fireflies circling its head.
reasoning:
I'm sketching the proportions for a forest spirit deer-like creature, planning a shoulder height around a meter with antlers reaching up to 1.7m, and starting to set up the builder structure for the model.

I'm defining the surface paints next—stone and moss mottle patterns, wood grain for legs and face, bright green eyes, and white flower/leaf accents—before working out the joint hierarchy for the spine, hips, and chest using a chain structure.

Then I'm sweeping the body along that spine chain with a tapered radius that flattens slightly and narrows toward the ends, followed by building a separate neck chain running from the chest up and forward toward where the head will sit.

For the neck chain with three names, the tip joint lands at t=1 as "head," placed at the top of the neck path and parented to the neck tip. For the face, I'll keep it simple with a flattened stick-like shape rather than a full lathe, representing it as a flattened ellipsoid attached to the head joint.

Working out the face geometry and antler placement now... I'm thinking of scaling a sphere unevenly to form the muzzle, positioned at the front of the head, then sprouting antlers as curved paths branching upward and outward from each side of the head joint using catmull-spline points.

For radius tapering along the antler, I'll pass an array of decreasing values so the beam thins toward the tip, and I'll use a proper Path object instead of a raw polyline so it curves smoothly. For branching tines off the main antler, I'm considering sampling a point along the antler sweep to get a frame, then sprouting a secondary branch from that frame.

Thinking through tip placement, I want to move outward along the frame's local axes to compute where each tine should point, settling on using the frame's offset method with up/forward values rather than constructing a full path — a simple tip point should work fine for the sprout call.

For the small flowers at antler tips, I'll attach tiny spheres using a stick helper that seats them onto the tip frame's axis. For leaves, I'm considering using a slab or extrude approach to build flat leaf shapes positioned along the tines, working out whether to pull in texture-based cards or just keep it simple with colored geometry.

Still working out leaf orientation...

For moss, I'm thinking of layering a second, slightly larger sweep over the body painted in a moss color to simulate patchy coverage.

For the body coloring, I'm defining a paint function that blends stone grey and mottled moss green based on surface normal direction and some noise, so moss appears more on upward-facing areas like a real creature would accumulate growth.

Now I'm setting up the four legs as chains running from hip or shoulder down to the hoof, using simple straight-point spans (thigh to knee to ankle to hoof) rather than full IK, keeping it slender and stylized like wood.

I'm sweeping these leg chains into tapered cylindrical shapes with wood coloring, then adding small dark cone-like cylinder parts at the bottom of each leg to represent hooves positioned right at ground level, and working out the specific coordinates for front versus hind leg placement on the chest and body.

Now I'm figuring out the body proportions overall — spine centered around a height of 1.0, legs attaching near the bottom, shoulders slightly higher, and the head/antlers rising up to around 1.9 — before moving to plan the glowing eye spheres on the head.

Then I'm positioning the glowing eyes symmetrically at the front of the head, and placing a small wooden mask shape slightly in front with carved eye hollows so the eyes peek through, adjusting depth so the mask sits just behind the eyes without clipping. I'm also sketching out a scatter of tiny glowing firefly spheres around the head for atmosphere.

Beyond that, I'm thinking about adding surface detail to the body: scattering small white flower sprigs and green moss tufts across the back using surface sampling so they sit naturally embedded in the mesh, giving the moss-painted body some physical relief rather than just flat color.

For the antlers, I want occasional leaf extrusions at tine tips, inheriting bone weights from the head so they move with the antler. I need to figure out the skull geometry too — the head is currently just a joint, so I should add an actual sphere or capsule mesh behind the mask to give it physical form, then build the antler main beam as a curved sweep rising from a base point near the skull.

I'm placing the antler origins on each side of the head, defining a short catmull path with tapering radius for the main beam, then adding tines branching off the sweep at specific points and angles using the sprout/moved helpers to position tine tips.

For the tine tips, I'm planning small white sphere flowers embedded at each tip, reusing the same computed tip point for both the tine sprout and the flower stick so they align correctly.

For the leaves, I'm extruding a flat quadrilateral outline lying horizontally at the tine tip, oriented so its normal points upward like a leaf resting on the antler, using sharp corners at the tips with slight smoothing for a natural curve. I'm planning two leaves at the tine tips plus one additional leaf partway along each antler for extra detail.

For fireflies, I'm placing five small yellow spheres at hardcoded positions floating around the head to suggest glowing insects, keeping them as separate loose objects rather than attaching them to a bone since they should appear to hover freely.

Now I'm defining the paint textures: a mottled stone pattern and a mottled moss pattern for the body, a wood-grain bark texture running along the legs, and a grain texture for a facial mask area, then combining moss and stone using a noise-based threshold on surface normals to create a natural mossy-stone blend across the body.

For the skeleton, I'm setting up a spine chain with joints for hips, waist, and chest, and I'm working through how to avoid duplicating the root joint by making the first spine joint act as the root itself rather than creating a separate pelvis joint.

I'll settle on "hips" as the root joint and build the spine chain from there, accepting the slight redundancy of overlapping points. Then I'll continue outward to a neck chain parented off the chest tip, laying out points that sweep upward toward the head.

The head joint sits at (0,1.4,0.6), with the head sphere and antler base positioned relative to it, and the neck gets a tapering sweep radius from the chest. I'm now adding the head sphere mesh itself, binding it to the head bone with a slight asymmetric scale for a more natural shape.

Next I'm placing the face mask as a hemisphere-like sphere offset forward slightly so it pokes out of the head just enough for depth, then positioning the eyes as small spheres just inside the mask's front curvature so they sit naturally in the hollow rather than poking through. Finally I'm sketching out the antler paths as catmull-rom curves branching upward and outward from the head, checking that the overall height doesn't make the antlers too tall relative to the body.

Now I'm working out how to build each antler symmetrically using a mirrored side parameter, sweeping a tapered radius along the curve with a wood-like color, and I'm noticing the sprout path needs to start exactly at the antler base rather than defaulting to the head joint's own center, which would otherwise prefix an unwanted straight segment.

Then I'm figuring out tine placement by sampling a point along the main antler sweep, offsetting it upward and forward to form the tip, and sprouting a smaller tapered branch from that sweep point so it inherits the correct bone weighting rather than rigidly following the head.

For tines I need unique joint names per side and index, so I'll use a naming pattern like `tineL${k}` since the single-span case only uses the given name directly. The antler chain names should follow sequentially (antlerL1, antlerL2, etc.) and stay unique, with the chain's parent correctly resolved to the head joint via boneFor.

Now I'm adding small spheres at tine tips as decorative stick elements, placing additional flowers along the antler at varying angles and lift heights, attaching leaves via extrude using positioned frames, and scattering decorations across the body surface using a filtered random distribution.

For each scatter hit I'm alternating between cone-shaped tufts and sphere-shaped flowers, checking that the geometry's embed offset correctly sinks the base into the surface, and confirming the scatter only applies to body hits, not neck or head. I'm also placing a few firefly spheres near the head and starting to define a leg-building function that sweeps a chain of points with tapering radii toward hoof tips.

Working out the hip/knee/ankle/hoof point chains for front and hind legs, verifying the hoof sits at the right height and that each leg chain is typed correctly as an array of point inputs with matching joint names and parent frame references.

For the leg geometry itself, I'm sweeping tapered radii from hip to hoof using bark-colored wood, then placing cylindrical hooves at the tip joints, each anchored by bone reference and positioned at the correct ground height and z-offset. For the torso, I'm planning a piecewise radius function along the spine chain that bulges in the middle and narrows toward the rear and front, giving the body a tapered horse-like silhouette.

Still writing body sweep...

For the neck, I'm applying a separate tapering sweep with decreasing radii from chest to head, keeping it consistent with the body's paint color and segment count, while the head itself is a simple sphere attached at the head joint. I'm also noting that part scale accepts either a single number or a vector, which I'll use for subtle asymmetric scaling.

Then I'm setting up the module structure with exported metadata and a default build function that constructs the builder, assembles all parts, and returns the root, importing helper functions like paint, mottle, grain, and noise for surface coloring and texture, along with checking type signatures for outline points used to define leaf shapes for foliage details.

Building out the firefly spheres with their glow color, then moving into the skeleton rig: setting up hip, spine, neck, and head joints with proper parent chains, and positioning the leg chains relative to the hips and chest joints.
